utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case IT-08-91-T, the Prosecutor versus Mico Stanisic and Stojan Zupljanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Good morning to everyone. As we all know, the gremlins have ensured that we have a late start this morning, so I would begin by asking for the appearances for the day, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Matthew Olmsted and Crispian Smith for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Slobodan Zecevic, Slobodan Cvijetic, and Eugene O'Sullivan appearing for Stanisic Defence this morning. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. For Zupljanin Defence this morning, Igor Pantelic and Dragan Krgovic. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. I would alert counsel and the Court Officers that, having regard to the late start, we will sit through till 12.05, which would have been the ordinary time for the second break, and then we should be back on track. Yes, could the witness be escorted into the courtroom, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Good morning to you, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: I expect it has been explained to you that it is for technical reasons that we had a late start this morning, so we regret any inconvenience that would have been occasioned you by just having to wait around. Before I invite Mr. Olmsted to resume his examination-in-chief, I would remind that you you're still on your oath. Yes, Mr. Olmsted.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-179 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Yesterday before we recessed, we were looking at a number of payroll records from SJB Vlasenica. Can you tell us where you would send these payroll records?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-179 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The payroll records were sent to the public security centre, because that's where the financial service was housed, which was in charge for the payroll for both the public -- or, rather, Security Centre and station.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And just so I have this clear, those payroll records, would they make their way up to the RS MUP headquarters?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-179 [Resumed]
utterances.text: We sent them to the public security centre, and they, in turn, received funds from the Ministry of Interior. In other words, the amount that was set aside for pay had to come from the Ministry of the Interior.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Now, during the May through December 1992 time-period, what means of communication did the SJB Vlasenica have with the CSB?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-179 [Resumed]
utterances.text: From May to December. If I may clarify this, the public security centre and the Ministry of Interior had a direct flow of information. Now for the public security station, according to the earlier organisation of the MUP.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, apparently further technical problems developed. Could you pause a moment, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Sorry, we are advised that we can proceed because the recording continues. In the meantime, we'll continue to work on the -- I mean, you probably see on the screen, but perhaps, Mr. Olmsted, out of an abundance of caution you should ask the witness to repeat his answer to your last question.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour, I'll do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Sir, sorry for the, again, a technical problem. I'll ask the question again and perhaps you could repeat your answer. During this May through December 1992 time-period, what means were available to SJB Vlasenica to communicate with the CSB Romanija-Birac?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-179 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Briefly, since the public security station under the earlier organisation of the MUP belonged to the security centre in Tuzla, all the rely and communications systems were directed to -- toward Tuzla and Sarajevo. On the 24th of April, as early as at that time, Vlasenica could no longer receive its -- electricity supplies from the grid in Tuzla. This problem prevailed for the following year, that's to say, until March of 1993. During that period the conventional communications means such as telephone lines and teleprinter lines and radio lines were -- were down. So, for an initial period of a month, roughly, the communication with the public security centre of Romanija and Birac was by way of couriers. In other words, a driver would show up on designated days and deliver mail, collect whatever mail there was in the station to take back with him. Subsequently, power supplies were enabled through two small electric plants that were in the possession of Vlasenica, and they powered certain essential services such as the hospital and the MUP. Therefore, thanks to the efforts of the communications workers of the MUP, first a telephone line was made operational, which could be resorted to, to communicate with the CSB and MUP whenever there was electricity. In parallel to this, the communications workers of the MUP also rearranged the relay system which had previously been directed toward Tuzla and Sarajevo to use them for these communications. This took a month to become up and running. After a period of some three to four months, the teleprinter communications were also made operational so that as of end of July or month of August, the communications systems improved, and, in fact, they continued to improve through to the end of the year.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: So if I understand from your answer you said the first month after the takeover there was problems with communications but by June, if I calculated correctly, you at least had a telephone line, whenever there was electricity available?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-179 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Whenever there was electricity available, telephone lines were used. But the teleprinter and radio communications, they could also be made operational only when there was electricity.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Now, during this same time-period, did you or members of your SJB leadership attend meetings with members of the CSB leadership?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-179 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The meetings were organised periodically and whenever necessary. But we had a meeting at least once a month, and that was a meeting of the chiefs of centres, and the meetings took place in Lukavica. Since Vlasenica is a transit town, occasionally information would be delivered there, whenever somebody happened to be passing in -- through that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Now, these meetings that you just described, would the SJB chiefs also attend those meetings?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-179 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And you mentioned that these monthly meetings were held in Lukavica. Were they ever held in Jahorina?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-179 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall exactly, but we may have had two meetings at Jahorina.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And when you met at Jahorina, where would you meet? What building?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-179 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I recall one meeting taking place in the Hotel Kosuta where the minister's office was temporarily housed at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: When you say "the minister," would that be the minister of the interior?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-179 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Now, at these meetings, these monthly meetings, what kind of information would be exchanged between the SJB chiefs and the leadership at the CSB?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-179 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The meeting of chiefs of the public security centre was always held according to a certain procedure. A report was submitted on public law and order. Security and traffic situation that was normally one of the items on the agenda. The other item would be the briefing on specific problems depending on the rapporteur and the area he covered, and the third item would normally be the resolution of certain problems or adoption of conclusions. That was the usual procedure adopted at such meetings in order for the chief of the centre to be fully appraised of the events having taken place in his area and of steps that had to be taken from his level.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And what would CSB Chief Cvijetic do with this information he collected from the various municipalities within his jurisdiction?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-179 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Normally, conclusions would be drawn from the minutes that were taken, which he would examine and forward to the Ministry of the Interior, and to the services directly under the minister, and to the minister himself.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Now, I would like to switch to a different topic. In the post-takeover period in Vlasenica - so after 21 April - what restrictions were imposed upon the freedom of movement of Muslims?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-179 [Resumed]
utterances.text: There weren't any explicit restrictions or orders. Any citizens who may still have been there, who did not leave, enjoyed a freedom of movement, though they did make sure to move about as little as possible. But as for any specific restrictions or orders to that effect, they did not exist.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Let's take a look at 65 ter 2808.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: This is a Crisis Staff document, subject is: "Instruction on General Procedure for Departure." And it's addressed to the chief of the public security station and the commander of the Territorial Defence. So would you have received this document from the Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-179 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since it existed there, it must have reached the station, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Now, under number 2, it says: "To leave the town, an individual has to sign a statement saying that he is leaving the town and ... territory of the municipality of his own free will; only on the basis of this statement will he be issued with a travel permit." Sir, towards which ethnic group did this particular requirement apply?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-179 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The request was valid for all the citizens who wanted to leave Vlasenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Yes. But in practical effect, who did it apply to?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-179 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Generally speaking, it was valid for all citizens, and I'll tell you why. This, in particular, applied to the departure of the Bosniaks. I presume that this was the idea entertained by the authority issuing this.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And what was the purpose of this requirement that Bosniaks would have to get this -- sign this statement that they were leaving the town voluntarily? What was the purpose of this statement?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-179 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I presume that the purpose was -- well, in that period of time nobody forced anyone else to leave. However, tensions were such that people were leaving, Serbs and Bosniaks alike. Now, I presume, since I'm not the author of the document, that, already at the time, the International Committee of the Red Cross had been present in the area and exerted pressure on the Crisis Staff, i.e., on the leadership, to provide an explanation for the fact that the people were leaving.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Well, I just want to be clear here. If I understand what you told us before, is that the practical effect of this instruction was that it applied to Bosniaks and not to Serbs; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-179 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mostly to Bosniaks. As for the Serbs, it applied mostly to able-bodied men and that's already we're dealing with item 3 of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Certainly. But we're only talking about item 2. Now, I assume that number 3 is an effort to keep Serbs in the municipality so that they can be mobilised. Number 3 talks about leaving and it's specifically saying that the individual has to sign a statement saying they're leaving of their own free will. And my question to you is: Was that or was it not applied to Bosniaks?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-179 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It applied to Bosniaks. The statement was signed in the municipality and we received the document. Whoever wanted to leave had to go and sign a statement in the municipality. They would be provided with a document, and could go wherever they wanted to.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Now, in what numbers were Muslims leaving Vlasenica during this time-period?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-179 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the stages of departure of citizens of Bosniak ethnicity from Vlasenica - yesterday we spoke about the Serbs and now we're focussing on the Bosniak population - was several. One of the stages of departure occurred shortly before the 21st of April. Already, as of the month of March, groups and individuals started leaving in the direction of Sarajevo and Tuzla, and some even ventured abroad. And in the period prior to the 21st of April, the process would be more intense at some points and less intense at others, because it depended on what was happening at the political level. Whenever a political compromise was achieved, then the intensity of departure would be lower, et cetera. So around the 21st of April the levels of departure intensified and the Crisis Staff organised buses for those who wanted to the leave. They would go to the bus station and would be transported to what -- at the time was still not a separation line in the direction of Tuzla, but it was a point that was already manned by the Green Berets or the BH police who would take the leaving population from there.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And who would escort these buses from the municipality to the BiH-held territories?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-179 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The buses were escorted by the police. There would be a police vehicle at the head of the column and a police patrol at the rear. If there was several buses in the column, that is. They would escort them to the place where they would be taken over by a different authority.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Now, what happened to the homes of the Muslims who left the municipality?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-179 [Resumed]
utterances.text: If nobody occupied these homes any longer, they were closed, abandoned, and empty.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Were Serbs moving into the municipality as Muslims were moving out?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-179 [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean into the houses or into the municipality?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Both.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-179 [Resumed]
utterances.text: After these events, after the 21st of April, refugees, as we could already call them that at that time, began flocking in under the control of what is now the Federation. Initially, this reciprocity was not that marked but later there was a marked reciprocity in this exchange so that later a large number of refugees came from what is now the territory of the Federation but then from the municipalities where Bosniaks were a majority. So they left those municipalities and sought accommodation in Vlasenica, Zvornik, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And let's answer the second part of the question is: When they would move to Vlasenica, where would they live?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-179 [Resumed]
utterances.text: There already existed a body in the municipality to receive this population. I don't know what it was called at the time. This organ had already made a list of the deserted, abandoned houses and flats, so by a kind of a decision they would assign them for temporary residence into those houses and flats.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Your Honour, may we tendered this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This would be Exhibit P1063, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Now, after the Serb takeover in Vlasenica on 21 April, were there takeovers in the surrounding Muslim villages?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-179 [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the first days, on the first day and in days that followed immediately, the taking over happened in the city of Vlasenica proper. Namely, according to the plan of those who did the taking over, on the first day, they occupied all the institutions and put them under their control. The SJB, the public security station, the municipality, the court, et cetera, in other words.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: I'm sorry to interrupt you, but I want to focus you because we do have limited time. My question was after the takeover on the 21st. So let's go beyond the takeover in Vlasenica town itself. After that occurred, were there other takeovers in the villages, the Muslim villages that surrounded Vlasenica town, within the municipality?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-179 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The Territorial Defence Staff had prepared a plan for taking over and establishing control of villages in Vlasenica municipality with emphasis on the seizure of illegally procured weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And what -- or which Serb forces participated in these takeovers?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-179 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The protagonist of this task was the newly established Territorial Defence Staff which was set up on the 19th of April, according to a decision of the Crisis Staff. Then the forces of the JNA that were present in the area which we already have referred to. And the police had the task or, rather, the Territorial Defence Staff and the army had the task of providing conditions for listing and seizing weapons, and this was done by the police which took the weapons to the station, because this was within police jurisdiction; namely, records on weaponry were.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Now when you say "police," do you mean the active police or the reserve police?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-179 [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that particular moment, as we said yesterday, this was mostly the active police force. There was a transformation in process, so a number of the reserve police force was also involved.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And could you tell us, what was the role of the special-purpose unit that we were discussing yesterday in these operations?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-179 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The special-purpose unit did not exist in the MUP. At that time it was part of the Territorial Defence. And it also participated in this mission of creating conditions for weapons to be handed over, collected, and put on a list, recorded.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Okay. But did these takeovers continue past the point where the special unit became part of the SJB; in other words, mid-May did these operations continue into the rest of May and also into June?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-179 [Resumed]
utterances.text: For the most part, according to the documents that I have available, this activity lasted until the end of May, on the basis of the plan of the Territorial Defence Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Now, did the Crisis Staff, the Serb Crisis Staff, play any role as far as organising, conducting these operations?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-179 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It did play a role, because on the 19th of April the Crisis Staffs set up the Territorial Defence by its decision and assigned these tasks to it. Namely, to create a plan of activities for the ensuing period.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Now, how was the SJB notified about plans to take over a particular Muslim village?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-179 [Resumed]
utterances.text: As this task was organised by the Territorial Defence, usually it would be within a specific time-period. Usually not longer than half a day. Information would be submitted to the SJB, to the effect that there would be activities undertaken in such and such an area. This was done for reasons of secrecy, or confidentiality.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Would you receive these notifications by fax?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-179 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sometimes by telefax. Mostly by fax. Sometimes it would be brought by courier.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Let's take a look at 65 ter 10290. Now, if the usher could just flip through the B/C/S pages, just one by one. Go to the next page. And just continue to go through that, just so that the witness can take a look at them very briefly.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Sir, --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Olmsted, is this document which obviously is -- well, I should is not on your 65 ter list, is it on your list of documents to -- for use with this witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Your Honour, this is the series of documents that we discussed at the beginning of the session yesterday, that Your Honours admitted onto our 65 ter list. These were the ones that were turned over during proofing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Oh. We didn't get the 65 ter numbers for those documents then.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: I apologise, yes. The correct number is ... yes the correct number is the one we just provided, 10290.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Sir, we flipped through these documents. Are these the documents that you recently provided to us?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-179 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Now, again, did you -- where did you find these documents originally?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-179 [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the same archives that I had.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: At the SJB building in Vlasenica?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-179 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Let's take a look at the first page. You've already been discussing the creation of the Territorial Defence. Do you recall when the VRS was established in the RS?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-179 [Resumed]
utterances.text: If we follow the orders, the order was for the Army of the Republika Srpska to be set up on the 12th of May. However, it was done somewhat later. I cannot remember exactly when. But I believe that it was after the 19th of May, after the decision according to which the JNA had to withdraw. So it was in the period until -- for instance, the 15th of June. Because I know that on the 28th of June, the Army of Republika Srpska emerged on the combat line towards Crska for the first time at a place called Logosi [phoen]. So if this happened on the 28th, they must have been organised at least seven days before that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And what happened to the Territorial Defence once the VRS was established?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-179 [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can recall, following this idea of the establishment of the Army of Republika Srpska, at a certain point an order was received from the level of either the Ministry of Defence or the President of the Republic to the effect that all Territorial Defence units should be transformed into the units of the Army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Now if we could go to page number 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And, sir, could you tell us if this is the kind of faxed notification that the SJB would receive prior to the takeover of a Muslim village? In this case, I think it's Turalici?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-179 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And you had a quick chance to review the ones that follow this one. Are they also examples of these kind of faxed notifications?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-179 [Resumed]
utterances.text: They are.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Now what would happen to the Muslims who would turn in their fire-arms to the police. What would happen to them next.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-179 [Resumed]
utterances.text: They could remain there. They could stay on and live there?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: During these takeover of Muslim villages, were there any paramilitary groups participating?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-179 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, most frequently, the Territorial Defence and the army unit would say be accompanied by a group - how shall we call it? - the Serbian Guard. Occasionally, a smaller group featured. They introduced themselves as men from Vukovar. With them, we, as the police, had problems. And after several days, we literally drove them out, expelled them from the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And what were these groups, these groups such as the Serbian Guard and the men from Vukovar, doing during the takeovers?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-179 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Initially, when they first came, they would say that they were this special unit or something like that, but later when we saw that their only motive was looting and different crimes we decided to expel them, and we literally expelled them at gunpoint.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: May this document or this series of documents be tendered into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: I assume there is no objection. Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: All of them at one time?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Yes, I believe he -- we talked about the first one and the second one and those that followed, he said, were simply other examples of notifications that he would receive with regard to operations in Muslim villages.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay. Mr. Olmsted, I'm still not -- still a little bit confused about those numbers. If I am right, the new documents you sent us by e-mail were 0674-7111, till 7115 and then other number -- till 116. And I don't see 110, which is the first one you showed the witness. How come I miss that?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: I don't know, Your Honour. In the e-mail we sent to everyone on the 9th of March at 5.35 p.m., we attached the documents and we note -- we said it was ERN 0674-7110 through 0674-7116. So that would include the whole range.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay. Then I missed one. Sorry, my mistake.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honours, I note that that Your Honour said there is no -- no objection, but we objected to these documents at the beginning of the session yesterday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, I realise that [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: I haven't forgotten your position on principle.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] I haven't forgot than at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And, Your Honours, I believe for the sake of clarity maybe it would be wise if we could have like 100.1, 2, 3, 4, because they are different documents, in order to distinct them, in a sense.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes. I was going ask whether the -- it's being admitted as a batch or as a series.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: And I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: So they're seven pages we understand. They will be given one exhibit number because otherwise it would simply complicate matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And we --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honours, the documents are -- are -- are different -- with a different dates and everything. I mean, it's not one document. It's -- it's a set of documents with different dates and -- referring to different places and -- they might be of the same nature, I agree with that, but I think it -- it should be -- it should be divided in -- in a -- by the numbers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: We don't need to -- to spend much time on this, but it's -- it's -- apparently it's either giving them seven individual consecutive exhibit numbers, or, since the documents are related and on the same subject, then put them altogether in one number.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I don't -- I don't think that it is achievable that we give them one number because those are the different documents. We might be challenging some of them with the -- with -- in our Defence case. So what I'm suggesting that we give it one number and for the each page we give it .1, .2, 3, 4.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: I inquired about that. That would create its own set of problems.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I was trying to be helpful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: So it seems that [Overlapping speakers] ... give it seven different numbers.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: May I make a suggestion, Your Honours, and I apologise, we got it at such a last minute that we weren't able to individually -- we call it MIF them, assign them separate 65 ter numbers, but what we can do is when we assign it one 65 -- one P number today, then we'll go back, we can fix it all, and we can notify the parties and we can sort it out that way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Then would you have to reserve seven consecutive exhibit numbers. The decision is we reserve seven numbers and then you get back to us with the correct ERN numbers and 65 ter list numbers.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: So 65 ter 10290 becomes P1064 through P1070, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Now, do you recall whether the police participated in the collection of weapons from the Muslim population in the villages of Drum and Piskavice?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-179 [Resumed]
utterances.text: One of these documents says that that activity also unfolded at Piskavice.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: I want draw your attention to a particular incident. Were you aware that during the takeover Drum, Muslim civilians were killed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-179 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was aware of the fact that it happened, but since you are insisting on this document, could you please tell me what date it is -- what date is on it, because I do not remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: I'm not referring to a particular document. I am just referring to an incident. Were you aware that Muslims living in the village of Drum were killed during the takeover of that village?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-179 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Specifically, in these actions, in these activities, there were no casualties. Only later, perhaps in June, there was a wider ranging army or Territorial Defence and army action, which encompassed, Piskavice, Drum, and Gradina and that is when such incidents happened. However, as part of these activities which are referred to in these documents, there were no consequences, there were no people killed. It was done in a peaceful way. Only later, perhaps on the 10th June there was a broader army and Territorial Defence action, purely military action, covering this entire area, because there were problems at the spot named Gradina which borders on Crska. Whereas in these activities referred to in these documents, there were no victims, not in a single of the villages. So we can say that that was so until the 30th of May. Only later in this action subsequently in June, we can check the exact date and that was a purely military operation. That is when there were victims in Drum and Piskavice.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Thank you very much for that very thorough explanation, but, again, please focus on the question, and perhaps I could have been a little clearer. I was moving on from the documents we looked at and just talking about Drum in particular. Now, who told you -- first of all, how soon after the killings in Drum did you learn about those killings?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-179 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps on the following day. A Bosniak came whom, by dent of circumstance, I happened to know. He worked at the forestry estate in Birac. He was in charge of occupational safety. He came about 9.00 or 10.00 in the morning to the station, and he knew me. And he told me what had happened. He told me that there were - I cannot say exactly at this point - eight or nine victims, and he sought police protection for a dignified funeral of the victims at the local cemetery. I talked to the commander, the komandir, and we provided such protection to them and this funeral took place at the local cemetery. He told at that moment, It is only the police that I can trust at this moment. And we really respected his request and this funeral went on in a dignified way. The surname of this person was Begic. I cannot recall his first name, but his last name was Begic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Did you send a criminal investigation team down to Drum to look into this incident?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-179 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did. But, at the time the crime police, rather, recorded all these cases, there were no conditions for a quality on-site investigation to be undertaken by the police at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Now, did you write a report, an information report, about these killings, to submit to the CSB?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-179 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that a dispatch or a report was also sent to the CSB reporting that there had been such and such action undertaken and that such and such things had happened in this specific area.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: To your knowledge, were the killings in Drum ever properly investigated and prosecuted?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-179 [Resumed]
utterances.text: In that period, we tried to document some things. But one must appreciate the fact that it was very difficult for a proper and intensive investigation to be undertaken at that time. The cases were registered. But later when the military organs, the military judicial organs were set up, we investigated a number of cases that we had collected. We actually submitted them, rather, to the Military Prosecutor's office for their action because we had problems at that time. If we wanted to interrogate, to question a member of the army, they would protest. They would say that we had no jurisdiction for that work because they were members of the army, so that all the reports that we had along these lines in July or August, when the military court and the Military Prosecutor's Office with their headquarters in Sokolac were set up, we submitted all these reports to these organs for their further action. The ministry, i.e., the police station, actually dealt only with cases, mainly with cases having to do with civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Page 21, lines 10 and 11, there is no distinction between question and answer. I would know it would be remedied after, but just to draw the attention. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Let's take a look at another document. This has been admitted as 1D183. I believe you might have had the right document. If you could bring that up. I thought it was the incorrect one. And perhaps turn to the second page of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Sir, if you could take a look at this document. Do you recall receiving this reminder in 1992?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-179 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, since the document was found in the archive, the answer is yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Can you tell us, was this TAS, T-A-S, vehicle theft issue a priority for the RS MUP back in 1992?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-179 [Resumed]
utterances.text: One of the tasks of the Ministry of the Interior, i.e., the police, is to prevent crime. One of the occurrences that was quite prominent was the theft of vehicles from the TAS factory. The Golf vehicle.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: What level of resources did you devote to carrying out this task of confiscating the TAS vehicles?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-179 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can you please repeat your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Yes. In 1992, what level of resources from the SJB did you dedicate to this task of investigating and confiscating these TAS stolen vehicles?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-179 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the police confiscated these TAS vehicles at check-points. Now, as for the records and analysis of documents, this was something that the crime service of the police did. In other words, the policemen manning check-points had to find out if a vehicle which was suspected of having belonged to the TAS was, indeed, that one, and if so, then it had to be taken to the police station. If it was found that a vehicle was rightful property of a private citizen then it would be given to the citizen. Otherwise, if it was found that it had belonged to the TAS factory, it would be confiscated and regulations that were in place would be applied from there on.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Was this considered dangerous police work, to confiscate these TAS stolen vehicles?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-179 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since there were dangerous combat activities taking place in an area, the confiscation of these vehicles was part of that dangerous work. However, the police had to perform their duties regardless of the risks involved. There were even attempts on the part of several paragroups to attack the policemen manning the check-points, and we had to engage in operations aimed at disarming them. I was involved in one such as well, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Now, during the May through December 1992 time-period, were the crime service police at SJB Vlasenica filing criminal reports with the basic prosecutor in Vlasenica?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-179 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The crime service police compiled documentation for all the occurrences of crime it could and wrote reports. Since, in the former BH, the court in Vlasenica had jurisdiction over places such as Milici, Sekovici, et cetera, from the period between April and August, there was only the President of the court appointed. Once the prosecutor's office was set up as well, and this was the case as of the month of August that the prosecutor was appointed, whatever we had of the potential case files, we handed them over to the prosecutor's office. Part of it was handed over to the Military Prosecutor, based on the agreement that had been reached on this issue with the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Let's take a look at 65 ter 2880. And if we could please not broadcast this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Sir, can you tell us - and perhaps we have a to scroll down a little bit - is this document signed by you? Or actually it's not signed by you. But was this report done by you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-179 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It probably was. Whenever such documents were transmitted via teleprinter, they would be transmitted without my signature. But I suppose I did, yes, write it.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Now, on the final line it says: "There have been no criminal reports against NN perpetrators." What does "NN perpetrators" mean?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-179 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Unknown perpetrators.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Now, according to this report, through the end of the July the SJB processed 108 illegal weapons cases. Against which ethnic group were these illegal weapons cases brought.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-179 [Resumed]
utterances.text: For the most part, illegal weapons possession involved members of Bosniak ethnicity, if one looks at the case register. Though there were others involved, most of them were Bosniaks.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Well, we're going to take a look at that crime register in a second. But you said "most." When you reviewed the crime register during proofing, were you able to find any illegal weapons cases against Serbs?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-179 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not, not on that occasion. I said the majority of the cases. What I meant was that the overall cases involved a number of members of other ethnicities, like Serbs, but as for the cases involving illegal weapon, they involved Bosniaks.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Can we tender this document under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked, under seal.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This would be Exhibit P1071, under seal, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Can we bring up what's been marked for identification as P1050. It was 65 ter 3563.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Sir, I think we've touched on this, but when the police would conduct investigative work into a crime, where would that matter be recorded?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-179 [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the crime register kept by the relevant station where the crime service was located.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Now, as we mentioned during proofing on Tuesday, you had the opportunity to review the crime register for Vlasenica. Well, can you tell us whether this is, in fact, the SJB Vlasenica crime register covering at least the period of April through December 1992?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-179 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is the conventional crime register which had to be kept.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: So if we could -- please take a look at page 43 in the English and B/C/S. And just in advance, perhaps we should not broadcast the portions of this book that are inside of it because it lists victims and such. Yes, and page 43 -- 43 of the B/C/S. I'm sorry, try 42. My numbering is off. There we go. And if you could zoom in on the writing -- yeah, exactly there.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: The portion we're looking at right now, it states: "182 concluding for 1992." What does this number, 182, signify?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-179 [Resumed]
utterances.text: This means that 182 crimes were recorded and processed. And this applies to various types of crime.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Can we now turn to page 2 of the B/C/S and the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Now, this page contains the first ten entries of the registry for the RS MUP, Vlasenica SJB. Can you just tell us generally, very briefly, what kind of information is contained in the various columns in this register?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-179 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot read it because the print is too small. But this is the typical information about who submitted the report, when, and against whom, type of crime, and reference to the relevant articles of law.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And if we can just keep it on the big B/C/S. Can we scroll down and look at the perpetrators that are listed here.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Can you tell me for these ten entries what their ethnicity is?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-179 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Bosniak.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Now, I think that you mentioned the criminal article on which they are charged is here, is that in column 12.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Maybe go up to the top and over as far right. There you go.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 213.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And what is an Article 213 case.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-179 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's under the criminal law of the former BH which was in application at the time, illegal weapons possession, manufacture and sale of weapons, ammunition, and such-like.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: So are these examples of the 108 illegal weapons cases that you reported in your 30 July 1992 letter that we just looked at?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-179 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Possession of the illegal automatic weapons or devices prohibited under the law.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Now, prior to filing one of these illegal weapons reports against a Muslim, would the police interrogate the Muslim?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-179 [Resumed]
utterances.text: For the most part, the evidence underlying criminal reports consisted of illegal weapons about which the police was notified. According to the criminal law procedure, the individuals involved would give a statement and the weapons would be confiscated, in order to serve as evidence in subsequent proceedings.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And where would these statements of the suspects be taken?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-179 [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the police station in the crime service premises.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Were you aware of instances in which some of these suspects, Muslim suspects, who were brought into the police station were either beaten or otherwise abused during their interrogations?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-179 [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the period when we were able to take control of matters, which was as of mid-June, all the actions taken had to in be in conformity with the criminal law procedure. As of the 21st of April through to mid-May or thereabouts, the station was predominantly under the control of paramilitaries and other groups. We were unable to take control. Until communications were established with the MUP of Republika Srpska and instructions received about the application of the Law on Criminal Procedure, this wasn't the case. But from then on, these provisions of law, like Law on Internal Affairs and criminal procedure law, had to be applied, and all these individuals that were brought in and interrogated had to be treated in accordance with the legislation.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: So prior to middle of May, were there instances where Muslims who were brought into the police station were beaten or otherwise abused?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-179 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot assert that, because I didn't have either the influence or the decision-making power. I didn't see anyone being mistreated, which does not rule out that possibility that it may have happened when I was away. In that time-period, paramilitaries would come there and do certain things until conditions were created for the station to be properly set up and act in accordance with the Law on Internal Affairs.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: You say that you didn't see any instances of beatings. Did you receive reports that Muslims were being beaten or abused at the SJB building?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-179 [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the period up until the 15th of May, I didn't have an incentive to submit any reports, because I was a nobody.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: I'm not talking about submitting reports. Did you receive reports? Did you hear reports? Did anyone come to you and say, Muslims are being beaten or abused at the SJB building? Up until May 15th.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-179 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There were stories around about people being beaten up, et cetera. We, who were members of the service, insisted with the President of the Crisis Staff, or wherever -- or, rather, not. We insisted with the president of the municipality that a way should be found for these groups that drew closer to the public security station to be removed.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Now, between the 15th of May and the middle of June, were you aware whether Muslims brought into the police station were being beaten or abused?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-179 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that, in this time-period, this was not the case. If such a case did occur, it wasn't either I or the co-ordinator from the crime service or the commander of the station who were informed of it, who knew about it. It was --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can the witness please repeat the last sentence he said.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Could you repeat your last sentence, please.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-179 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It could have happened in the absence of any one of us who had, at that time, had authority at the station; the komandir, me, as the co-ordinator, or the head of the crime service. This may have been facilitated by some reserve policemen who, as soon as we found out about these cases, would be chased out of the station and turned over to the Army of Republika Srpska. This was the only thing we could do with these individuals.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: When you received any information about these incidents of abuse at the SJB building, would you report these incidents to the CSB?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-179 [Resumed]
utterances.text: You see, once the communications system was up and running, via the teleprinter, every day information relating to the events of the preceding day would be sent out. It was called the bulletin of daily events, and these bulletins must certainly contain all the events of the previous 24 hours. In other words, they would be informed about any unlawful events and pressure experienced by the station and its forces, which was constant, because these were groups who wanted to flout the law and exercise their own law. They felt that now the time has come -- had come for them to be the law, when the war was on. We always had the threat from them. We would come into conflict with them. The station would be surrounded and attacked by them. However, we never gave up on the principle that we should abide by the law and that the station should be part and parcel of an institution which aspired to do its job professionally in the service of all citizens. This was how we conducted ourselves. All the anomalies that occurred - and I'm referring to your earlier questions - they may have occurred. But we responded to each and every one such occurrence. From processing any possible policeman who may have been involved, applying procedures and sanctions that were in place against such policemen who considered themselves to be prominent Serb fighters. It was very difficult, you see, to apply any measures against them because they enjoyed the support among the population at large and those who stood behind them, and we were confronted with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Thank you for that thorough explanation, but please, please, try to focus on the question. The way the procedure works here is I ask a question and you focus on the question. At the end of these proceedings, I think that the Trial Chamber will give you an opportunity to say whatever you want. But for now, please, limit your answers to the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Can we look at the next page of this log-book, this register, or, actually, look at page 4. And if can you look at the second entry and if you could scroll over to the right of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: It says it's an Article 36 case. What kind of case is that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-179 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Believe me, when I tell you that I don't recall what is regulated by Article 36.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Okay. After 21 April what kinds of crimes were being committed against the Muslim population in Vlasenica? Just very generally.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-179 [Resumed]
utterances.text: After the 21st of April, most of the Bosniaks citizens had left Vlasenica. In the first and critical month or two, there were attempts at crime, such as murder, et cetera. The police took any and all measures it had within its competence.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Excuse me, sir.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-179 [Resumed]
utterances.text: However, despite the circumstances prevailing, we tried to prevent crime.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Again, please, focus on the question. You had a chance to review the crime register that's in front of you for the April through December 1992 time-period. Were you able to identify in this register any criminal reports where the victim or injured party was a Muslim or Croat person?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-179 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not in this crime register. The reason being that when the -- as I already said before, when the military court and the Military Prosecutor's Office were set up, we sent all these reports to them for their further action. This part of the crime register refers to civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: May we tender this crime register under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: P1050 is admitted, under seal.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Let's take a look at 65 ter 2886. And, again, please don't broadcast this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Sir, can you look at the signature. And can you tell us whose signature that is on this document?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-179 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is my signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Now, in the first paragraph you write: "Please find attached forms RZ and RZ-1 with information about war criminals and the act of genocide committed against the innocent Serbian civilian population in the territory of Vlasenica municipality." Was this letter that you wrote in response to a particular request for such information?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-179 [Resumed]
utterances.text: This document came from the ministry or from the security centre, and this is a covering letter with the RZ and RZ-1 forms, meaning that the covering letter is accompanied by these forms which were filled in, which I do not have now.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: So if I understand, your answer is that you were asked to collect evidence of war crimes against Serbs?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-179 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Now, it states in the second paragraph that you filed three criminal reports against perpetrators of war crimes against the Serbian population. With whom did you file those criminal reports?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-179 [Resumed]
utterances.text: These criminal reports were filed with the prosecutor's office in Vlasenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: That would be the basic prosecutor's office in Vlasenica?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-179 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: May we tender this one under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked, under seal.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That would be Exhibit P1072, under seal, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, the previous document in the record is P1050? Is that right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: It was MFI'd before. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: I want to move on to another topic now.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Was there a municipal prison in Vlasenica in May, June, July of 1992?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-179 [Resumed]
utterances.text: In view of the fact that the municipal court in Vlasenica was -- had jurisdiction for the area, Sekovici, Han Pijesak, et cetera, even before the war, there was a prison facility attached to the court.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Now just focussing on the May through December 1992 time-period, members of what ethnic group were being detained at that facility?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-179 [Resumed]
utterances.text: As that facility was not within the competence of the MUP, the police station, but within the competence of the court, according to my information, in that period, the persons who were detained there were of Bosniak ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Who provided security at that prison facility?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-179 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Security was the duty of the court. The employees of the court. But, at that time, the only employee of the court was the President of the court, because it was in the process of being set up. There was a lad in the court, Branislav Sokanovic, who had just come from Sarajevo and who was also in Sarajevo in charge of prison security, so here, also, he was immediately put in charge of prison security. He then prepared a plan for the security service, the guards' service. Initially, because of the shortage of staff to be engaged a certain number of policemen were put on guard duty, whereby -- and when the conditions were created for this to be resolved, otherwise we stopped providing that service, because it was under the jurisdiction of the Ministry of Justice and in agreement with the Territorial Defence, or somebody else, they set up a group of lads to provide security for the prison.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Did you ever visit the prison during this time-period?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-179 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I never visited it.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Why not? Your police officers were guarding the prison.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-179 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not because from the very moment that I was in a position to exert any influence whatsoever, I was against it. I wrote a letter to the Ministry of Justice asking them to resolve the status of that prison and of security. And after better communication was established with the CSB and the Ministry of Interior, I was given instructions to the effect that that was exclusively within the jurisdiction of the Ministry of Justice and that the police were no longer to provide this - shall I say so - service, providing security for the prison and we stopped doing that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: You said you wrote to the Ministry of Justice. When you wrote to the Ministry of Justice, would you provide a copy of your letter to the minister of the interior?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-179 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably. A copy was required to be sent to the chief of the security centre, and it was up to him to assess whether to refer that document onwards or not, or to communicate in relation to its content in another way.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Well, you wouldn't communicate with the Ministry of Justice without telling your superiors that you were doing so; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-179 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Normally I -- no, I communicated with the chief of the centre, and I told him I'm going to write a letter to the Ministry of Justice and state my problem. Namely, we are discontinuing this form of co-operation. This is their facility and let them state their view, or just abolish the facility or do whatever they pleased.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Let's move on to another document.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: This has been already admitted into evidence. It's P994.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, when you pulled out of the guarding of the prison in Vlasenica, who then took over after the police? Who guarded the -- the camp after that, or the prison after that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Later, after this young man who had been -- taken over, who had experience with prison security, the Ministry of Defence mobilised, assigned a number of people to do that job. Namely, just like I asked for police through the Ministry of Defence, they asked for men to be assigned to them for the purpose of securing the facility. That was the procedure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: So they were not soldiers or military police. They were just ordinary people who were hired for the purpose?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I suppose that Ministry of Defence assigned those who were less capable, in military terms, to tasks of this nature.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: I'm not sure what this means. Were the new guards at the prison in Vlasenica military people? Or were they just civilians who were contracted to guard the prison?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. There were no contracts in that period. What could be done was mobilisation through the Ministry of Defence, and I presume that the Ministry of Defence assigned less able-bodied men, maybe elderly men, older men, to these tasks. That would be usual.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Just a follow-up question on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Do you recall what month you wrote to the Ministry of Justice about this prison?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-179 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you see, all the activities aimed at establishing legality as much as possible unfolded towards the end of May and in June when there were already some indications that I and my colleagues would be confirmed by the ministry. So I proceeded, step by step, to try and put the situation in order. So this problem could also have been on the agenda more or less in June -- July. In July. Before that, I also talked to the President of the municipality, Mr. Stanic, and he also agreed. He absolutely agreed that this should be resolved because he realised that we had a problem. We had a problem of the shortage of good quality policemen, and, secondly, this institution was not within our jurisdiction, to begin with.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Perhaps that's a good place to stop.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes. We resume in 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Olmsted, I wonder if there is a possibility that we can clarify just one little issue in relation to the testimony that our witness gave just prior to the break. Because I am not sure I fully understood the reasons why he decided that the police should pull out of the guarding of the prison in Vlasenica. That's one issue. And the other issue was -- that I did not fully understand, was, that, when the police pulled out, was it then the Ministry of Justice who took over, or was it the Ministry of Defence? Mr. Witness, can you clarify those two issues.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: We cannot hear the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Firstly, why did we insist for police to pull out as security of this facility? Simply because this is a facility of the judiciary; of another institution, in other words. Prior to the war, this facility was not guarded by the police of the Ministry of Interior but by the court's own security. Every institution, even in those conditions which obtained at that time, was to do its own task. That's one thing. Can you just remind me of your second question. Oh, yes, yes, I've just remembered. After mobilising people to be -- as security guards, this task was taken over by the court. But they just wanted the Ministry of Defence to allow themselves -- them to undertake the necessary procedure, just as I did when I wanted to mobilise policemen for the reserve police force, because these were war conditions. So this was a way in which to obtain extra personnel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you. This is clarified.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And if can you just take note of the -- the document you are responding to, which is 01-127-92.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: If we can turn to the second page.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And we see on the second page there's a paragraph that states further down. It says: "One centre for accommodation of persons from the combat zone has been registered in the area of the public security station [sic]." Could you tell us what centre of accommodation you're referring to?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-179 [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the Susica reception or holding centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Let's bring up 65 ter 380. And if we can turn to the second page of each.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Can we turn to the third page of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Could you tell us who this is signed by.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-179 [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a document of the chief, Zoran Cvijetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: May that be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This would be Exhibit P1073, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honours. The previous document, I'm not sure that it -- what is the reference of the previous document that the witness commented?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Well, I think that's clear. He said that this document is a response -- or the prior document is a response to this one.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. But we didn't -- we didn't got the reference, at least in the transcript, of that prior document, and I'm wondering if it has been exhibited or what is the 65 ter number. That's only what I -- what I'm inquiring. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: I'll answer that. It has -- it has been admitted in evidence. It's P994, was the prior. Is this ...

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Maybe I misunderstood counsel's question. The one that we're looking at right now was 65 ter 380 and now it's been admitted, I believe, under a P number. Is that what -- Mr. Zecevic, is that what you were concerned about?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: No, no, no. Thank you very much. My reference -- my question was aimed at P994. That is the reference that I was missing. Thank you very much. I appreciate it.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: All right. Could we have 65 ter 2810 up on the screen. And please do not broadcast this one.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Sir, can you tell us who signed this document?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-179 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And which holding centre does this report relate to?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-179 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Susica.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Now you write in the first paragraph that the basic purpose of this holding centre is to receive people, both Muslims and Serbs, who have expressed a desire to leave Vlasenica. Can you tell us, how many Serbs were held at Susica camp?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-179 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The holding centre was established sometime after the 21st of April by a decision of the municipal organs in order to house inhabitants who wished to leave the territory of the municipality according to the principles that we discussed earlier. Their transportation to a specific point in the direction of Kladanj was also organised. However, as the number of those wishing to leave Vlasenica increased, during the day, not all of them could be transported, and someone, the Crisis Staff, or someone else, decided that they should be put up in the Territorial Defence facilities in Susica until there were conditions for their transportation at the latest by the next morning when there would be buses to transport them. So Bosniaks were put up there who wished to leave Vlasenica. Later, when we say that Serbs were accommodated there in the combat, around Gorazde, there was a period, sometime later, when a large number of Serbs started leaving the area, and they, too, were put up there until the time when a -- the political situation was resolved. Let me not belabour the point now. They wanted to go to Serbia but were not allowed and later were, and so on and so forth. Furthermore, during the fighting between Croats and Bosniaks in Bosnia, the political leadership of the then Herceg-Bosna and of Republika Srpska agreed that they can cross the territory of Republika Srpska safely towards Serbia, and from then onwards wherever they wanted to go via Hungary or Croatia and so on. So they, too, were accommodated there until the conditions were created for all of them to be transferred to their final destinations. So at a certain period -- in different periods there were Bosniaks and Serbs and Croats in this holding centre, but not all of them at the same time.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Thank you for your -- again, for your thorough answers. I know that you're really trying to provide as much information as possible, but please keep your answers focussed on the question. Can you tell us in what month the Serbs arrived at Susica camp, if you recall in -- if it was 1992.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-179 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that it was sometime in August or September.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Now you write -- and you've just mentioned that holding centre is under the authority of the municipal organs. Can you tell us what municipal organs you're referring to?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-179 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Crisis Staff and the Territorial Defence, and, later, with the setting up of the VRS, this came under their jurisdiction.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Now, the report also mentions that the camp held persons captured in the zone of war. At the beginning of June 1992, do you recall this Susica camp receiving a number of Muslim men from Sekovici?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-179 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not from Sekovici but from the zone towards Kalesija. I do remember because until then this holding centre was really of a humanitarian nature, to accommodate civilians who wished to stay there up to the time when, in combat operations in June, from the zone towards Kalesija, a number of prisoners -- of military prisoners of war were put there. And, at the time, the army definitely took over all competences over them. Before it was under the Territorial Defence but from that point everything was under the army. I do not have the document, but there were orders on the setting up of what was later called a camp and the procedures to be applied, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Can you tell us what happened to those prisoners? Were they transferred anywhere?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-179 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They stayed there for a month or so. I can't be more precise than that. At that point, I insisted, once again, for a way to be found for these individuals to be transferred. In conversations with Mr. Stanic, President of the municipality, I insisted, for reasons of safety and security, that he, as a higher authority, should intervene with the competent military or political structures, in order to have these individuals transferred. A month later, through his offices and higher authority, Mr. Stanic managed to have these individuals transferred to Bijeljina, to a camp there, which went by the name of Batkovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: You said you insisted that these prisoners be transferred somewhere else. Why are you insisting on that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-179 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Purely for security reasons. Broadly speaking, I could not conceive of the existence of camps in the what was to be the 21st century.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Olmsted, had you requested four hours with this witness. You have now exceeded that by ten minutes. How much longer do you think you would be?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Half an hour, just because I want to cover a few more documents and a couple more topics with this witness that no one else will be able to cover. I apologise for that. I should have applied for that earlier.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Did you convey your views up your chain of command to the CSB, about this camp?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-179 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. I conveyed my views to the Chief Cvijetic, and I presume that he informed the ministry or minister accordingly. Because results were achieved. And the idea was that within the public security station [as interpreted], attempts should be made to -- attempts were made to prevent this from happening.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Did you ever visit Susica camp yourself while it was in operation?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry to interrupt, but I believe the witness said "the ministry," line 17, page 44. "The idea within the ministry," and maybe this can be clarified with the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Well, I think that will be corrected once they fix the transcript, so let's move on given my limited amount of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Were you -- I think you answered that you have never visited -- you never visited Susica camp during this time period?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-179 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. For reasons of principle. I rather tried to solve the problem at levels I believed this could be solved.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Were any incidents of beatings or killings at Susica camp reported to you, or did you learn about them from any sources?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-179 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Personally, I didn't have reliable information to the effect that there were such occurrences over there, such as murder or beatings. I heard about these activities subsequently through statements given by witnesses, et cetera. The police didn't have any authority over there. I even -- or I forbade the police from going over there, unless we were required to get involved, according to the scenario produced by the army, in case the camp came under attack or similar situations.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: May we tender this document under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, admitted under seal and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This would be Exhibit P1074, Your Honours, under seal.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Now, we're going to try to move very quickly through the next remaining topic so that we can finish in time.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Can that be -- I guess, admitted and marked under seal, for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, admitted and marked, under seal.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This would be Exhibit P1075, under seal, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Now, do you recall Minister Stanisic ever coming through Vlasenica in 1992?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-179 [Resumed]
utterances.text: On his way to Belgrade, the minister had to go via Vlasenica, but he never stopped by. I never had occasion to receive him in my station. Rather, I would receive reports from check-points that Minister Stanisic had gone past.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Sir, during our interview last year, you mentioned that there was an occasion in either June or July 1992 when Mr. Stanisic came in his vehicle and you had a conversation with his driver. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-179 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Can you describe what happened on that occasion. What his driver told you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-179 [Resumed]
utterances.text: We discussed paramilitaries. One group of paramilitaries, the so-called Zute Ose were in Vlasenica, Angry Wasps [as interpreted]. The earlier minister had problems with them. They man handled him and so on.
